name: Nano Banana AI Image Editor
tagline: Browser tool for generating and editing images from natural language prompts, built on Google's Gemini image model.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: This is a web front end over Google's Gemini image model, the one everyone calls Nano Banana. The front end itself is a one-sitting build: upload an image, type an instruction, show the result, keep a local history. What you cannot build is the model, so your personal version still calls Google's API and you pay Google per image instead of paying a reseller per credit. That is usually cheaper and always more transparent, but it is a hard third party dependency, which is why this is a kinda and not a yes. If you want something with zero external calls you are into local diffusion models, which do not follow edit instructions nearly as well.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app that takes an image plus a text instruction, sends both to the Gemini image API with your own key, and shows the edited result with a saved history.
requirements: A Google AI Studio API key with billing enabled
Willingness to pay Google per generated image
whatYouLose: Prepaid credit bundles and someone else eating the API billing complexity
Hosted gallery, shareable links, and anything that works from a phone without you deploying it
Curated prompt presets and example galleries that teach you what the model is good at
Someone else absorbing model version changes, rate limits, and safety rejections
Any guarantee the app still works when Google renames or deprecates the endpoint
moatNotes: The proprietary model is Google's, not this site's. The site rents the same thing you can rent, which makes convenience and pricing the entire product.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a credit pack is a simpler purchase than a cloud billing account, and most people editing a photo once a month do not want to think about API keys at all. Wrapper sites also do the unglamorous work of handling uploads, aspect ratios, retries, and safety refusals so the first attempt actually produces something. That is real value, it is just not defensible value: the moment the underlying model gets a decent first party UI, the markup gets hard to justify.
notes: The interesting part of this product is a model someone else trained and rents to anyone with a credit card.
prompt:
Build a local-only AI image editor called "banana-local" in an empty folder.

Stack, non-negotiable: Vite + React + TypeScript on the front end, a small Express server in the same repo as an API proxy. No database, no auth, no accounts, no telemetry, no analytics.

Behavior:
1. Single page. Left side: a drop zone that accepts one image (png/jpg/webp, max 10MB) plus an optional second reference image. Right side: result viewer.
2. A textarea for the edit instruction, plus a Generate button. Support text-to-image too: if no image is uploaded, the prompt alone is sent.
3. The Express route POST /api/edit forwards the prompt and any images to Google's Gemini image generation endpoint using model id "gemini-2.5-flash-image" and returns the generated image as base64. Read GEMINI_API_KEY from process.env. Never expose the key to the browser.
4. Show real errors verbatim in the UI, including safety refusals and rate limits. Do not swallow them into a generic "something went wrong".
5. History: persist every generation (thumbnail, prompt, timestamp, model id) in IndexedDB via idb-keyval. Clicking a history item reloads its prompt and result. Add a Download button and a Clear history button.
6. Iteration loop: a "use result as input" button that feeds the output image back into the input slot so edits can be chained.

Out of scope, do not build: user accounts, credit systems, Stripe, hosted deployment, sharing links, prompt template galleries, masking or inpainting brushes, batch queues.

Deliverables: package.json with dev script running Vite and the Express server concurrently, .env.example containing GEMINI_API_KEY=, a README with setup steps and a one-line note that image generation costs real money per call, and .gitignore covering .env.

Keep the UI plain: system font stack, one accent color, no component library. Working beats pretty.
